parts.title: Olvasott szöveg értése
parts.name: The rise of the repair café
parts.text:
In a community hall in Bristol, a retired engineer is examining a broken toaster while its owner watches nervously. Ten minutes later, the toaster is working again, and the owner has learned how to replace a fuse. This is a repair café, one of more than two thousand that now operate around the world.

The idea began in Amsterdam in 2009, when a journalist called Martine Postma decided that throwing away broken objects had become far too normal. She organised a single event where volunteers with practical skills offered to fix things for free. The response was so enthusiastic that she soon set up a foundation to help other communities copy the model.

Supporters say repair cafés do much more than reduce waste. Visitors often arrive feeling frustrated with products that seem designed to fail, but leave feeling more confident about understanding the objects they own. "People are surprised by how simple many repairs are," says one volunteer. "Often it's just a loose wire."

There are limits, however. Many modern devices are glued together or need special tools, and manufacturers do not always make spare parts available. Campaigners argue that new laws are needed to give consumers a genuine "right to repair". Several countries have recently introduced rules forcing companies to supply parts and repair manuals for a number of years.

For now, the cafés rely on volunteers, donated tools and a great deal of goodwill. But as one regular visitor puts it, "You don't just fix your kettle here. You meet your neighbours."

parts.title: Olvasott szöveg értése
parts.name: The myth of multitasking
parts.text:
Few skills are more widely admired in the modern workplace than the ability to multitask. Job advertisements routinely request it, and many of us take quiet pride in answering emails during meetings or drafting reports while monitoring a stream of messages. Yet a growing body of research suggests that what we call multitasking is, in most cases, something rather less impressive.

Neuroscientists point out that the brain does not genuinely perform two demanding tasks at once. Instead, it switches rapidly between them, and each switch carries a cost. Attention must be withdrawn from one task and re-engaged with another, and in the process small amounts of time and accuracy are lost. Over a working day, these losses accumulate into what some researchers estimate to be a reduction in productivity of up to forty per cent.

Perhaps more troubling is the finding that habitual multitaskers tend to overestimate their own abilities. In laboratory studies, those who reported multitasking most frequently often performed worse at filtering out irrelevant information than those who rarely did so. The very habit that people believe sharpens their minds may, paradoxically, be dulling them.

None of this means that all combinations of activity are equally harmful. Listening to music while running, or chatting while cooking a familiar dish, places little strain on our cognitive resources, because one of the activities has become largely automatic. The difficulty arises when both tasks require conscious thought.

Some organisations have begun to respond. A number of firms now encourage "focus hours" during which notifications are switched off and meetings are banned. Early reports are cautiously positive, though critics note that such schemes depend heavily on managers modelling the behaviour themselves. A policy announced by email and then ignored by senior staff is unlikely to change anything.

parts.title: Olvasott szöveg értése
parts.name: The four-day school week
parts.text:
When a small rural district in Colorado announced that its schools would close every Friday, many parents were horrified. Who would look after the children? Would they fall behind? Five years later, the four-day week has become so popular that more than a hundred districts in the state have followed the same path.

The original reason was money. Running buses and heating buildings one day less each week saved the district around seven per cent of its budget, which allowed it to keep teachers it would otherwise have lost. Recruitment also improved: teachers were attracted by the promise of a long weekend, and fewer of them left for better-paid jobs in the cities.

The effect on learning is harder to measure. Some studies have found small drops in test scores, particularly in maths, while others show no difference at all. Researchers point out that the school day becomes longer when the week is shorter, and tired pupils may not get as much out of the final hour.

Families are divided. For parents who work on Fridays, the extra day can mean paying for childcare. Yet many pupils use the time well, taking part-time jobs, helping on family farms or attending sports clubs. Some schools now offer optional Friday activities for those who need them.

What seems clear is that the four-day week works best where the community supports it. As one headteacher put it, "It isn't a magic solution. It's a trade-off, and every town has to decide whether it's worth it."

parts.title: Olvasott szöveg értése
parts.name: Why we keep things we never use
parts.text:
Open almost any kitchen drawer and you will find it: the strange tool nobody remembers buying, the charger for a phone thrown away years ago, the takeaway menus from restaurants that have long since closed. Most of us own far more than we need, and yet the idea of getting rid of things makes many people uncomfortable.

Psychologists have a name for part of this behaviour: the endowment effect. Once we own something, we value it more highly than we would if we were thinking of buying it. In one famous experiment, people who had been given a coffee mug asked for about twice as much money to sell it as others were willing to pay for the same mug.

Memories play a role too. A ticket from a concert or a jumper knitted by a grandparent is not really about the object itself. Throwing it away can feel like throwing away a piece of our past. And then there is the classic thought: "I might need it one day." Occasionally we do, which convinces us that keeping everything is sensible.

The decluttering movement argues that this habit has a cost. Crowded homes can be stressful, and searching for lost items wastes time. Its supporters suggest simple rules, such as removing one object for every new one that comes in, or photographing sentimental items before letting them go.

Critics reply that there is nothing wrong with a little mess, and that a perfectly tidy home can become an obsession of its own. Perhaps the real question is not how much we own, but whether our possessions make our lives easier or harder.

parts.title: Olvasott szöveg értése
parts.name: The myth of multitasking
parts.text:
We like to think of ourselves as accomplished jugglers, answering emails while listening to a podcast and keeping half an eye on a group chat. Yet a substantial body of research suggests that what we call multitasking is, for the most part, an illusion. The brain does not genuinely perform two demanding tasks at once; it switches rapidly between them, and each switch carries a cost.

These costs are small enough to escape notice, which is precisely what makes them insidious. A fraction of a second lost here, a moment of reorientation there, and over the course of a day the cumulative effect can be considerable. Studies in which participants alternate between simple tasks consistently show slower performance and more errors than when the same tasks are completed one after the other.

Intriguingly, those who consider themselves skilled multitaskers often perform worst. In one widely cited experiment, heavy media multitaskers were more easily distracted by irrelevant information and slower to switch between tasks than their less habitual counterparts. Confidence, it seems, is no guarantee of competence.

This is not to say that all combinations are equally problematic. Walking while talking, or listening to familiar music while doing routine housework, poses little difficulty, because at least one of the activities requires minimal conscious attention. The trouble begins when two tasks compete for the same mental resources, such as reading and listening to speech.

The practical implications are hardly revolutionary, but they are frequently ignored. Grouping similar tasks, silencing notifications during periods of concentrated work and resisting the urge to check messages the moment they arrive may feel inefficient. In reality, they allow us to do one thing properly rather than several things badly.

parts.title: Olvasott szöveg értése
parts.name: In praise of boredom
parts.text:
Few experiences are as universally disparaged as boredom. We fill every idle moment with our phones, treat waiting rooms as an opportunity to clear our inboxes, and regard a child who complains of having nothing to do as a problem to be solved. Yet a growing number of researchers argue that boredom, far from being a pointless discomfort, may serve a genuine purpose.

The argument runs roughly as follows. Boredom is an unpleasant signal that our current activity is failing to engage us. Like hunger, it prompts us to look for something more rewarding. Without it, we might remain stuck in unproductive situations indefinitely. In this sense, boredom is less an absence of feeling than a nudge towards change.

There is also evidence linking boredom with creativity. In one study, participants who first completed a deliberately tedious task, copying numbers from a telephone directory, subsequently came up with more inventive uses for a pair of plastic cups than those who had skipped the dull activity. The researchers suggested that a wandering mind, freed from external stimulation, is more inclined to make unusual connections.

None of this means that boredom is always beneficial. Chronic boredom has been associated with poorer mental health and risky behaviour, particularly among adolescents. The distinction appears to lie between brief, occasional boredom, which can be productive, and a persistent sense that life lacks meaning.

What may be lost in an age of constant entertainment is the first kind. If every pause is instantly filled, the mind never has the chance to drift. The challenge, perhaps, is not to eliminate boredom, but to tolerate it long enough to see where it leads.

parts.title: 1. szöveg
parts.name: The history of the pencil
parts.text:
The modern pencil owes its existence to a chance discovery in the 1560s, when a large deposit of unusually pure graphite was found in Borrowdale, in the north of England. Local shepherds reportedly used it to mark their sheep, and it soon became clear that the material left a darker, cleaner line than lead, which had been used for writing since Roman times.

Because pure graphite was soft and brittle, early users wrapped it in string or sheepskin. The idea of enclosing it in wood is generally credited to Italian craftsmen, who hollowed out sticks of juniper and inserted a graphite core. The design proved so practical that it has changed remarkably little since.

The Borrowdale mine was so valuable that it was guarded and flooded between extraction periods to deter thieves. When supplies elsewhere were cut off during the Napoleonic Wars, the French engineer Nicolas-Jacques Conté developed a method of mixing powdered graphite with clay and firing the mixture in a kiln. By varying the proportion of clay, manufacturers could produce pencils of differing hardness, a system still used today.

Despite the arrival of ballpoint pens and digital devices, the pencil has retained a surprising number of loyal users, from architects and artists to astronauts, who value its reliability in conditions where ink might fail.

parts.title: 2. szöveg
parts.name: Urban heat islands
parts.text:
On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island effect, arises mainly because materials such as asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly at night. The lack of vegetation compounds the problem, since plants cool their surroundings through the evaporation of water from their leaves.

The consequences extend beyond discomfort. Higher temperatures increase demand for air conditioning, which in turn raises energy consumption and emissions. During heatwaves, the effect can be deadly: elderly people and those with heart or lung conditions are particularly vulnerable, and studies of past heatwaves have found significantly higher death rates in the hottest urban districts.

Cities have experimented with a range of countermeasures. Reflective 'cool roofs' painted in light colours can lower roof surface temperatures considerably. Green roofs, covered with plants, offer additional benefits such as absorbing rainwater, although they are more expensive to install and maintain. Planting street trees remains one of the most cost-effective options, provided that species are chosen carefully to withstand drought.

Urban planners increasingly argue that such measures should be coordinated rather than introduced piecemeal. A single green roof makes little difference; a network of parks, trees and reflective surfaces across an entire district can measurably reduce temperatures.

parts.title: 3. szöveg
parts.name: Can animals count?
parts.text:
For much of the twentieth century, claims that animals could count were treated with suspicion, largely because of the case of Clever Hans, a horse that appeared to solve arithmetic problems by tapping its hoof. It was later shown that Hans was responding to tiny, unconscious cues from his questioners, who relaxed when he reached the correct number. The episode made researchers extremely cautious about interpreting animal behaviour.

Modern studies, however, use carefully controlled methods to rule out such cues. Experiments have shown that a wide range of species possess what scientists call 'number sense': the ability to judge which of two groups contains more items. Fish, for example, prefer to join the larger of two shoals, and honeybees can be trained to choose the card showing a particular number of shapes.

This ability is generally approximate rather than exact. Animals distinguish easily between three and six objects, but find it much harder to tell twelve from thirteen. Interestingly, human infants show a similar pattern before they learn to use number words, suggesting that this approximate system may be an ancient and widely shared feature of animal brains.

What appears to be uniquely human is the use of symbols to represent exact quantities. Some chimpanzees have learned to associate numerals with quantities after extensive training, but there is little evidence that any animal spontaneously develops such a system. Counting, in the precise sense, may therefore depend on language and culture as much as on biology.

questions.why: "responding to tiny, unconscious cues from his questioners"

questions.why: "human infants show a similar pattern"
